label: Peace and Calm
framing: The peace Scripture offers is not mainly the absence of conflict but the presence of a wholeness, the Hebrew shalom, things set right with God, with others, and within. It is a peace given rather than achieved, one that does not depend on the storm stopping and that Jesus said the world cannot give.
cultural: Shalom in the Hebrew Scriptures meant far more than quiet; it named a flourishing rightness, the whole of life knit together as it should be, fields fruitful, debts forgiven, the stranger safe, the relationship mended. It was a public and social thing, not merely a private calm, and the false prophets were condemned for crying peace, peace, where there was no peace, papering over a brokenness they would not name. To seek shalom was to seek the repair of the whole fabric, not just a settled feeling in oneself.
historical: The church received peace as a gift before a task, greeting one another with it and passing it across the table at the Lord's Supper. Augustine, watching an empire collapse in the fifth century, defined peace as the tranquility of right order, a thing the City of God held even as the city of man fell. The long tradition of Christian peacemaking, from the early refusal of the sword to the believers who reconciled enemies across blood feuds and battle lines, treated peace as something made, not merely wished for.
application: Inner peace usually follows from bringing the thing you are carrying to God rather than turning it over and over alone, so pray it specifically and let the request leave your hands. Make peace where you have broken it, since the unsettled conscience and the unrepaired relationship steal more rest than any circumstance. Guard the inputs that agitate you, the endless feed of alarm, and choose stillness on purpose. And remember that the peace promised is not a calm you manufacture but a presence that guards you while the trouble is still real.

verses.text: Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid.
verses.where: On the night before he dies, Jesus leaves his disciples his peace, a gift unlike anything the world gives, and tells them not to let their hearts be troubled or afraid. The site's plain note says he spoke to friends who were rightly afraid, on the worst night of their lives, and gave them his peace, not a lecture. It adds that do not be afraid is not a rebuke of people who live with anxiety, panic or fear.

verses.text: Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
verses.where: Paul tells the church to bring everything to God by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, and says the peace of God, which surpasses understanding, will guard their hearts and minds. The site's plain note says he gives a practice, not a switch, and promises God's peace, not that every request will be granted as asked. It also says Paul himself admits to sorrow and anxiety elsewhere in his letters.

verses.text: ‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.’
verses.where: The LORD gives Aaron and his sons the words to bless Israel: that the LORD would bless and keep them, make his face shine on them, and give them peace. The site's note on the chapter says the blessing places God's name on his people. Peace here is something God gives when he turns his face toward someone.

verses.text: Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God.
verses.where: Paul says that those justified through faith have peace with God through Jesus Christ, and stand in grace. The site's plain note asks whether a person lives as one who stands, or as one always afraid of being thrown out. Peace with God comes first in Paul's order, before peace of mind.

verses.text: Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful.
verses.where: Paul tells believers to let the peace of Christ rule in their hearts, since they were called to it as members of one body, and to be thankful. The site's note on the chapter sets this among compassion, kindness, humility, forgiveness and love. In Paul's words the peace that rules the heart is also the peace that holds a church together.

verses.text: But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!” And the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm.
verses.where: A fierce storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps in the stern, and his disciples wake him asking whether he does not care that they are perishing. The site's note says his sleep comes not from flight from God but from trust in him, and that stilling the sea is something only God does in Israel's Scriptures. The plain note says their deepest fear was that Jesus did not care.

verses.text: They dress the wound of My people with very little care, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all.
verses.where: Through Jeremiah the LORD says the prophets and priests dress his people's wound with very little care, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace. The site's note says their words did not address sin: they reassured people without calling them to change. A quiet bought by pretending the wound is not there is not the peace Scripture means.

verses.text: But the LORD said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die.” So Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and called it The LORD Is Peace. To this day it stands in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verses.where: Gideon, a frightened farmer threshing wheat in a winepress, is afraid after meeting the angel of the LORD, and the LORD says to him, Peace be with you; do not be afraid. Gideon builds an altar and calls it The LORD Is Peace. The word of peace comes before any battle is won.

verses.text: Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field. The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. Then my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest.
verses.where: Isaiah says that when the Spirit is poured out, justice will dwell in the wilderness, the work of righteousness will be peace, and God's people will live in secure places of rest. The site's note on the chapter says the desolation lasts until that outpouring, bringing justice, righteousness, peace and rest. Peace in the prophets grows out of things being set right.

verses.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.
verses.where: Jesus calls the peacemakers blessed, for they will be called sons of God. The site's note says the beatitude blesses not those who love peace but those who make it, and points ahead to his command to love enemies. Peace between people is work to be done, not only a mood to be hoped for.

misread.taken: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword is used to justify harshness, picking fights, or cutting off family in Jesus' name, as if peace were not a Christian concern.
misread.says: The site's plain note says it is a picture of division, not a call to violence: Jesus describes what his coming will do, as some follow him and some do not. He told Peter to put his sword away, he called the peacemakers blessed, and no one may use this verse to justify harming anyone, inside a family or outside it. The note adds that it is not a command to cut off your family, and that the division comes from others' response to him, not from a follower's harshness.
misread.text: Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.

whole: Many people who pray for peace mean quiet: the argument over, the bills paid, the test results back, the mind finally still. Some try to keep the peace at home by never saying what is true, and find that the silence costs them something. Some look for calm in a break, a breathing exercise or a different job, and find that it does not last past the next piece of bad news. Others feel guilty that they are not at peace, because they have been told that a real Christian would be.

Scripture's peace is larger than quiet. The priests' blessing asks that the LORD would turn his face toward his people and give them peace, and Isaiah says peace is the work of righteousness, when justice dwells in the land. Peace in the Bible begins with God: Paul says those justified through faith have peace with God through Christ. It reaches between people, so that the peace of Christ is to rule in a church as members of one body, and Jesus calls the peacemakers blessed. And it reaches into the heart, where the peace of God guards hearts and minds. Part of why we lack it is that we look for it in the wrong order, wanting a quiet mind without peace with God, or quiet in the house without the truth that real peace needs. Jeremiah's prophets cried peace, peace when there was no peace, and dressed a deep wound lightly. Most of us have done the same with our own wounds, and with other people's.

So the Bible's wisdom is to receive peace before trying to manufacture it. Paul tells the Philippians to bring everything to God in prayer with thanks, and the site's plain note calls that a practice, not a switch; what he promises is God's peace, not that every request will be granted as asked. Jesus left his own peace with his friends on the worst night of their lives, and gave it without a lecture. Peace with others is to be made, not only hoped for, and making it may mean saying a hard true thing gently rather than swallowing it. And where worry or fear has become an illness of body and mind, the site's notes say plainly that it needs care, not blame, and that getting help is not a lack of faith.

The hope Scripture gives is that peace is a person before it is a feeling. Jesus slept in the stern of a boat in a storm, and when his frightened friends asked whether he cared, he rose and spoke to the wind. Gideon, hiding his wheat in a winepress, heard the LORD say peace be with you before any battle was won, and named his altar The LORD Is Peace. The storm may not stop the moment you pray. But the one in the boat with you is not afraid of it, and his peace is given, not earned.
deep.sit: Where are you keeping the peace by staying silent about something true, and what would it look like to bring it to God, and then to the person, gently?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note points to verse 8: before the promises of peace, someone chose to listen. Pray it slowly, and leave room to listen.
prayer.text: I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly. Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him, that His glory may dwell in our land. Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed.
